title: Impact of Compulsory Schooling on Wages

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
The research question aims to identify the causal impact of additional compulsory schooling on individuals' wages later in life. Given the presence of an instrumental variable (compulsory schooling year, z), we can use the Instrumental Variable (IV) method to address potential endogeneity issues in the relationship between education (x) and wages (y). The key assumption for the IV method is that the instrumental variable (z) affects the outcome (y) only through its effect on the treatment (x), and not through any other channels. This is known as the exclusion restriction. Additionally, the instrument must be relevant (i.e., it must be correlated with the treatment) and not be affected by the same factors that affect the outcome (instrument exogeneity).

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load necessary libraries
library(readr)
library(plm)
library(AER)

# Read the data from the CSV file
data <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s68_data.csv")

# Convert the data into a pdata.frame for panel data analysis
# Since this is a cross-sectional dataset, we set the individual index to a constant
data-paneled <- pdata.frame(data, index = c(1:nrow(data)), drop.index = TRUE)

# Estimate the first stage of the IV model
first_stage <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = data)

# Estimate the second stage of the IV model using 2SLS
second_stage <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls, data = data, subset = NULL, 
                       instruments = ~ z + controls, 
                       clusters = NULL, weights = NULL)

# Print the coefficients of the second stage
summary(second_stage)

# Basic robustness checks
# Check if the instrument is relevant (first stage F-statistic)
first_stage_fstat <- summary(first_stage)$fstatistic
print(paste("First stage F-statistic: ", first_stage_fstat))

# Check for overidentifying restrictions (not applicable here since we have one instrument)
```

## 3. Expected Findings
We expect a positive coefficient for the effect of education on wages, indicating that additional compulsory schooling leads to higher wages. The magnitude of the effect will depend on various factors, including the quality of education, individual characteristics, and labor market conditions. Given the log-linear specification, the coefficient represents the percentage change in wages associated with a one-year increase in education. Based on previous studies, the estimated effect might be in the range of 5-15% return to education, although this can vary widely depending on the specific context and data.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use compulsory schooling year as an instrument for education.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The analysis suggests that additional compulsory schooling has a negative impact on log wages.
